prompt: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget, and explain how they relate to each other.
answer_markdown: An SLI is a Service Level Indicator: a measured ratio of good events over valid events, such as the proportion of requests returning a non-5xx status within 300ms. An SLO is the Service Level Objective, the target for that SLI over a stated window, such as 99.9% over 28 rolling days — and without a window the SLO is meaningless, because 99.9% over an hour and over a quarter are entirely different promises. The error budget is simply 100% minus the SLO: the failure you have explicitly permitted, roughly 40 minutes per 28 days at three nines. An SLA is a different kind of thing altogether: a commercial contract with customers carrying financial penalties. The relationship that matters in practice is that the SLA should be deliberately looser than the SLO, because if you promise 99.5% externally while targeting 99.9% internally, your internal alerts fire long before you owe anybody a refund. Setting them equal means your first warning and your first breach of contract are the same event.

prompt: Why should availability be measured as a ratio of events rather than as uptime?
answer_markdown: Because a running process is not a working service. A server can be up, passing its health checks, and returning 500 to every real request, which uptime records as perfect availability. Uptime also cannot express partial failure, and partial failure is what nearly all modern outages actually look like: one endpoint broken, one region degraded, 4% of users unable to check out. A ratio of good events over valid events handles all of those naturally, because a degraded state simply moves the number rather than forcing a binary up-or-down judgement. The discipline it demands is defining both halves explicitly — whether a 404 or a 429 counts as good, and whether health checks and internal load tests belong in the denominator — and that denominator is worth scrutinising, since it is where teams accidentally flatter themselves by excluding inconvenient traffic.

prompt: Why does burn-rate alerting beat a static error-rate threshold?
answer_markdown: A static threshold is wrong in both directions simultaneously. Set it at 1% and a thirty-second spike to 2% pages someone at 3am for something that consumed a rounding error of budget, while a sustained 0.9% error rate sits quietly underneath and drains a 99.9% service's entire monthly budget in about three days without ever firing. Burn rate fixes this by normalising against the budget: it is the observed error rate divided by the rate the SLO permits, so a burn rate of 1 spends the budget exactly over the window and 14.4 spends it in under two days. Because the metric is now denominated in budget consumption, the alert threshold expresses a real consequence rather than an arbitrary number. The production refinement is multiple windows — a fast-burn alert on a short window that pages for catastrophes and a slow-burn alert on a long window that tickets the quiet leak — with each pairing its long window against a shorter one that must also still be burning, which is what stops an alert firing for an hour after a two-minute blip already recovered.

prompt: Your service calls three dependencies, each with a 99.9% SLO, and all three are required to serve a request. Product wants to advertise 99.99%. What do you say?
answer_markdown: That it is arithmetically impossible. Availability composes multiplicatively across hard dependencies, so 0.999 cubed is about 0.997, or 99.7% — and that is the ceiling assuming your own code never fails at all, which is already below the three nines you might have assumed, let alone four. There are only three honest ways to raise the ceiling. Reduce the number of hard dependencies on the critical path. Add redundancy inside a dependency so its own availability improves. Or convert a hard dependency into a soft one by designing a fallback, so that its failure degrades the response instead of failing it — a recommendation service that falls back to showing bestsellers drops out of the multiplication entirely. This is the concrete argument for graceful degradation, and it is why the number of things that must work is itself an architectural decision.

prompt: What is an error budget policy, and why is it the point of having an SLO at all?
answer_markdown: An error budget policy is a rule agreed with product owners before anything breaks: while budget remains the team ships at normal pace and may take deliberate risks, and when the budget is exhausted feature work stops in favour of reliability work until the window recovers. It is the point because an SLO nobody acts on is just a dashboard. Without the policy, reliability loses every argument it has — a vague worry about risk against a concrete customer deadline — until enough incidents pile up that the team overcorrects into a freeze. With it, the recurring velocity-versus-stability conflict is settled in advance by a number both sides agreed to, so nobody relitigates it mid-incident. It also aligns incentives properly, because the product owner now has a direct stake in reliability: unreliability is what stops their features shipping. And it legitimises risk in the other direction, since spending budget you have is exactly what the budget is for.

prompt: Why must a latency SLO specify a percentile and a threshold rather than an average?
answer_markdown: Because an average conceals the tail that motivated the measurement. A service where 90% of requests take 50ms and 10% take 2.5 seconds has a mean of roughly 295ms and passes an 'average under 300ms' target comfortably, while one user in ten has a genuinely bad experience. Stating it as '95% of requests complete within 300ms' makes the target a ratio of good events over valid events, which slots into the same error-budget machinery as an availability SLO and cannot be gamed by fast requests subsidising slow ones. Many teams define two thresholds — 95% under 300ms and 99% under one second — so that both the typical experience and the worst experience each have a target, since a single percentile leaves everything beyond it unconstrained.

prompt: Should a team aim for 100% availability? And why is alert fatigue treated as a reliability problem rather than an annoyance?
answer_markdown: No. Each additional nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more in redundancy, review and operational caution, while the perceived benefit flattens out: at five nines you have about twenty seconds of budget per month, so any response involving a human is already a breach and the system must heal itself unassisted. Meanwhile a mobile user's own network drops far more often than that, so they cannot distinguish four nines from five. The right target is the least reliability at which users are happy, leaving the remaining budget available to spend on shipping. Alert fatigue is a reliability problem because it degrades the detection system itself: every page that turns out to be nothing teaches responders that pages are usually nothing, and that lesson is retained, so a team paged repeatedly for harmless blips will eventually miss the real incident. A noisy alerting system is therefore worse than a quiet one, because on top of missing things it supplies false confidence that someone is watching.
